Singapore's OCBC Bank didn't wait for a major fraud incident to overhaul its defenses. It rebuilt the system before it needed to.
OCBC was the first bank in Singapore to deploy AI and machine learning to combat financial crime, and the first in the country to launch its own dedicated AI unit. The problem they were solving was unglamorous but real. Compliance analysts were manually reviewing hundreds of potentially suspicious transactions a day, with complex cases taking up to a week to clear. In a market where scam payments can clear in seconds, that lag is the whole ballgame.
The bank built a Fraud Surveillance System into its Operational Risk Management program, designed to catch abnormal transaction patterns and protect customers even in cases where, technically, the customer is liable for authorizing the transaction themselves. That distinction matters. A huge share of scam losses today come from victims willingly approving payments under manipulation, not stolen credentials. Catching that requires behavioral pattern detection, not just rule-based checks.
In an earlier machine learning pilot on transaction monitoring, OCBC reduced false positive alerts by 35 percent and organized roughly 4,200 alerts into 48 distinct risk clusters, letting compliance teams prioritize by actual risk instead of working a flat, first-in, first-out queue.
The result was not one dramatic save. It was a structural shift, from analysts drowning in undifferentiated alerts to a system that tells them which fires to fight first. That is what mature fraud defense looks like. Not a single AI model catching one clever attacker, but infrastructure that compresses response time across thousands of transactions a day, so the next attack, whatever form it takes, gets caught in seconds rather than a week later.
Banks that are still running alert queues on a first in first out basis are not behind on AI. They are behind on triage.

comment: The harder challenge is often governance around AI decisions—ensuring models stay explainable, monitored for drift, and trusted by analysts when unusual patterns emerge.
